title: The School of Antioch
subtitle: A short Life and the surviving exegetical fragments
source: Life material adapted from Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History IV.25 (NPNF Series II Vol. 3, public domain). Exegetical fragments preserved by St. John Chrysostom and in the Antiochene catenae; English drawn from the standard nineteenth-century editions in the public domain.

sections.title: The lay teacher who became a bishop
paragraphs: Diodore was born around the year 320 in Antioch of a Christian family of senatorial means. He studied at the philosophical schools of Athens, where he became proficient in Aristotelian logic and in the secular rhetoric of the day, before returning to Antioch in his early twenties to teach the rudiments of biblical interpretation. With his friend St. Flavian (the future patriarch of Antioch), he organized the lay anti-Arian community of the city through the long pressure of the Arianizing emperors.

He took monastic tonsure and was ordained presbyter by St. Meletius of Antioch around the year 360. As a presbyter he led the public worship of the Nicene community of Antioch during the periods of Meletius's exile, when the cathedral was closed against the bishop's return. Among his pupils in his small school of biblical interpretation, taught privately in his presbytery house, were the young John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

He was exiled by Valens in the early 370s to Armenia, where he passed several years in the school of St. Basil the Great. On the change of imperial policy under Theodosius in 378, he returned to Antioch and was elevated to the see of Tarsus in Cilicia, the metropolitan see of his patriarchate, which he held for the last twelve years of his life.

He came to the Second Ecumenical Council in 381 as one of the Council's leading theological voices on the side of the Meletian, Nicene party. After Meletius's death during the Council, his weight was felt in the canonical settlement of the new Eastern patriarchates and in the recognition of the rightful succession at Antioch. He returned to Tarsus and held the see for twelve more years until his death around 390.

sections.title: The exegetical method
sections.framing: Most of Diodore's writings have been lost in the polemical wake of the later Nestorian controversy (Diodore's pupil Theodore of Mopsuestia became, posthumously, one of the principal targets of the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and works associated with that school were widely destroyed). What survives is fragmentary. The two short selections below give the substance of his exegetical principles as carried forward by St. John Chrysostom.
sections.citation: Fragments preserved in the Antiochene catenae and in Chrysostom's Homilies on Genesis
paragraphs: We do not deny the higher senses; but we will not seek them where the letter has not first been served. The Scripture has many depths, but the foundation of all of them is the historical sense which the inspired writer himself intended; and to read what is not there in the foundation is to build on no foundation at all.

When the prophet speaks of Sion and of Jerusalem, let us hear Sion and Jerusalem before we hear the Church, and then let us hear the Church the more clearly because we have first heard the city. The figurative interpretation is the fruit, not the root. The fruit, when it is grown, takes its shape from the root which is the letter, and not from the air.

sections.title: The teacher of St. John Chrysostom
paragraphs: Chrysostom himself, in his sixth Homily on the Statues at Antioch, names Diodore among his teachers and calls him "a man rich in the divine learning, whose lips poured forth honey from the hive of the Scriptures." The principal achievement of Diodore's pastoral work was not his own surviving writing but the formation of the next generation of Antiochene exegetes, of whom Chrysostom is the chief; and through Chrysostom, the manner of reading the Scriptures, the literal sense disciplined by the rule of faith and oriented to preaching, has carried through the whole later Eastern tradition.

sections.title: Apolytikion of St. Diodore of Tarsus (Tone 4)
paragraphs: Hierarch Diodore, lamp of the divine wisdom and pillar of the Antiochene Church: you taught the divine Scriptures rightly to the Golden-Mouth and his fellow disciples, and confessed the Nicene Faith without yielding. Intercede with Christ our God that our souls may be saved.
